3. Data Transformation¶

As we see from the above results, the columns "season", "holiday", "workingday" and "weather" should be of "categorical" data type. But the current data type is "int" for those columns.

Let us transform the dataset in the following ways:

  • Create new columns "date", "hour", "weekDay", "month" from "datetime" column
  • Coerce the datatype of "season", "holiday", "workingday" and "weather" to category
  • Drop the datetime column as we already extracted useful features from it
In [404]:
season_map = {1: "Spring", 2: "Summer", 3: "Fall", 4: "Winter"}

weather_map = {
    1: "Clear + Few clouds + Partly cloudy",
    2: "Mist + Cloudy, Mist + Broken clouds, Mist + Few clouds, Mist",
    3: "Light Snow, Light Rain + Thunderstorm + Scattered clouds, Light Rain + Scattered clouds",
    4: "Heavy Rain + Ice Pallets + Thunderstorm + Mist, Snow + Fog"
}

def extract_date(dt_string):
    return dt_string.split()[0]

def extract_hour(dt_string):
    return dt_string.split()[1].split(":")[0]

def extract_year(dt_string):
    return dt_string.split()[0].split("-")[0]

def get_weekday_name(date_string):
    return calendar.day_name[datetime.strptime(date_string, "%Y-%m-%d").weekday()]

def get_month_name(date_string):
    return calendar.month_name[datetime.strptime(date_string, "%Y-%m-%d").month]

def transform_features(df):
    """Extract and transform features from datetime column."""
    df = df.copy()
    df["date"] = df["datetime"].apply(extract_date)
    df["hour"] = df["datetime"].apply(extract_hour)
    df["year"] = df["datetime"].apply(extract_year)
    df["weekday"] = df["date"].apply(get_weekday_name)
    df["month"] = df["date"].apply(get_month_name)
    df["season"] = df["season"].map(season_map)
    df["weather"] = df["weather"].map(weather_map)
    return df.drop(columns=["datetime"])

def convert_to_category(df, columns):
    """Convert specified columns to category dtype."""
    df = df.copy()
    for col in columns:
        df[col] = df[col].astype("category")
    return df

categorical_cols = ["hour", "weekday", "month", "season", "weather", "holiday", "workingday", "year"]

train_df = (train_df
    .pipe(transform_features)
    .pipe(convert_to_category, categorical_cols))

test_df = (test_df
    .pipe(transform_features)
    .pipe(convert_to_category, categorical_cols))

4.3 Outliers Analysis¶

At first look, "count" variable contains lot of outlier data points which skews the distribution towards right (as there are more data points beyond Outer Quartile Limit). Following inferences can be made from the boxplots below:

  • Spring season has got relatively lower count. The dip in median value in boxplot gives evidence for it.
  • The boxplot with "Hour Of The Day" is quite interesting. The median values are relatively higher at 7AM - 8AM and 5PM - 6PM. It can be attributed to regular school and office users at that time.
  • Most of the outlier points are mainly contributed from "Working Day" than "Non Working Day".

4.4 Correlation Analysis¶

One common way to understand how a dependent variable is influenced by features (numerical) is to find a correlation matrix between them.

  • temp, atemp and humidity features have positive and negative correlation with count respectively.
  • windspeed is not gonna be really useful numerical feature and it is visible from its correlation value with "count".
  • Since "atemp" and "temp" have strong correlation with each other, meaning one of them should be dropped during model building
  • "Casual" and "Registered" are not taken into account since they are leakage variables in nature and need to be dropped during model building.

4.5 Visualizing Distribution Of Data¶

As it is visible from the below figures that "count" variable is skewed towards right. It is desirable to have Normal distribution as most of the machine learning techniques require dependent variable to be Normal. One possible solution is to take log transformation on "count" variable. After the transformation the data looks lot better but still not ideally following normal distribution.

4.6 Visualizing Count Vs (Month, Season, Hour, Weekday, Usertype)¶

  • It is quite obvious that people tend to rent bike during summer season since it is really conducive to ride bike at that season. Therefore June, July and August have got relatively higher demand for bicycle.
  • On weekdays more people tend to rent bicycle around 7AM-8AM and 5PM-6PM. As we mentioned earlier this can be attributed to regular school and office commuters.
  • Above pattern is not observed on "Saturday" and "Sunday". More people tend to rent bicycle between 10AM and 4PM.
  • The peak user count around 7AM-8AM and 5PM-6PM is purely contributed by registered users.

5. Model Building¶

5.1 Data Preparation¶

Before building models, we need to:

  • Save test datetime for submission
  • Drop leakage columns (casual, registered) - they sum to count and are not available in test data
  • Drop date column - we already extracted useful features from it
  • Log-transform the target variable (count) to handle right-skewness
  • Convert categorical variables to dummy variables for linear models
In [417]:
test_datetime = pd.read_csv("test.csv")["datetime"]

# Drop leakage columns, date, and atemp (highly correlated with temp)
drop_columns = ["casual", "registered", "date", "count", "atemp"]

y_train = np.log1p(train_df["count"])

X_train = train_df.drop(columns=drop_columns)
X_test = test_df.drop(columns=["date", "atemp"])

X_train = pd.get_dummies(X_train, drop_first=True)
X_test = pd.get_dummies(X_test, drop_first=True)

X_test = X_test.reindex(columns=X_train.columns, fill_value=0)

print(f"X_train shape: {X_train.shape}")
print(f"X_test shape: {X_test.shape}")
print(f"y_train shape: {y_train.shape}")

5.2 RMSLE Metric¶

The Kaggle competition uses Root Mean Squared Logarithmic Error (RMSLE) as the evaluation metric.

In [418]:
def rmsle(y_true, y_pred):
    """Calculate RMSLE between actual and predicted values."""
    return np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))

5.3 Model Training and Evaluation¶

For each model, we will:

  1. Train on the full training set
  2. Calculate RMSLE on training data
  3. Show actual vs predicted comparison on training data
  4. Show distribution of predictions on test data
In [419]:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

def evaluate_model(model, model_name, X_train, y_train, X_test):
    """Train model, evaluate on train, and predict on test."""
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    
    y_pred_train = model.predict(X_train)
    y_pred_test = model.predict(X_test)
    
    train_rmsle = rmsle(y_train, y_pred_train)
    
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=1, ncols=3, figsize=(18, 5))
    
    # Plot 1: Train actual vs predicted distribution
    sns.histplot(np.expm1(y_train), kde=True, ax=axes[0], label="Actual", color="blue", alpha=0.5)
    sns.histplot(np.expm1(y_pred_train), kde=True, ax=axes[0], label="Predicted", color="orange", alpha=0.5)
    axes[0].set_title(f"{model_name}: Train Distribution")
    axes[0].set_xlabel("Count")
    axes[0].legend()
    
    # Plot 2: Train actual vs predicted scatter
    axes[1].scatter(y_train, y_pred_train, alpha=0.3)
    axes[1].plot([y_train.min(), y_train.max()], [y_train.min(), y_train.max()], "r--", lw=2)
    axes[1].set_xlabel("Actual (log)")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("Predicted (log)")
    axes[1].set_title(f"{model_name}: Train Actual vs Predicted")
    
    # Plot 3: Test predictions distribution
    sns.histplot(np.expm1(y_pred_test), kde=True, ax=axes[2], color="green")
    axes[2].set_title(f"{model_name}: Test Predictions Distribution")
    axes[2].set_xlabel("Predicted Count")
    
    plt.suptitle(f"{model_name} - Train RMSLE: {train_rmsle:.4f}", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    
    return y_pred_train, y_pred_test, train_rmsle

Ridge Regression¶

In [421]:
def ridge_objective(trial):
    alpha = trial.suggest_float("alpha", 0.001, 100, log=True)
    model = Ridge(alpha=alpha)
    scores = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    return -scores.mean()

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)
ridge_study = optuna.create_study(direction="minimize", sampler=TPESampler(seed=42))
ridge_study.optimize(ridge_objective, n_trials=30, show_progress_bar=True)

print(f"Best Ridge params: {ridge_study.best_params}")
ridge_model = Ridge(**ridge_study.best_params)
y_pred_train_ridge, y_pred_test_ridge, rmsle_ridge = evaluate_model(ridge_model, "Ridge Regression", X_train, y_train, X_test)

def lasso_objective(trial):
    alpha = trial.suggest_float("alpha", 0.0001, 1, log=True)
    model = Lasso(alpha=alpha)
    scores = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    return -scores.mean()

lasso_study = optuna.create_study(direction="minimize", sampler=TPESampler(seed=42))
lasso_study.optimize(lasso_objective, n_trials=30, show_progress_bar=True)

y_pred_train_lasso, y_pred_test_lasso, rmsle_lasso = evaluate_model(lasso_model, "Lasso Regression", X_train, y_train, X_test)

Random Forest¶

In [423]:
def rf_objective(trial):
    params = {
        "n_estimators": trial.suggest_int("n_estimators", 100, 500),
        "max_depth": trial.suggest_int("max_depth", 10, 50),
        "min_samples_split": trial.suggest_int("min_samples_split", 2, 10),
        "min_samples_leaf": trial.suggest_int("min_samples_leaf", 1, 4),
        "random_state": 42,
        "n_jobs": -1
    }
    model = RandomForestRegressor(**params)
    scores = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=3, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    return -scores.mean()

rf_study = optuna.create_study(direction="minimize", sampler=TPESampler(seed=42))
rf_study.optimize(rf_objective, n_trials=20, show_progress_bar=True)

print(f"Best Random Forest params: {rf_study.best_params}")
rf_model = RandomForestRegressor(**rf_study.best_params, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
y_pred_train_rf, y_pred_test_rf, rmsle_rf = evaluate_model(rf_model, "Random Forest", X_train, y_train, X_test)

XGBoost¶

def xgb_objective(trial):
    params = {
        "n_estimators": trial.suggest_int("n_estimators", 100, 500),
        "learning_rate": trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 0.01, 0.3, log=True),
        "max_depth": trial.suggest_int("max_depth", 3, 12),
        "subsample": trial.suggest_float("subsample", 0.6, 1.0),
        "colsample_bytree": trial.suggest_float("colsample_bytree", 0.6, 1.0),
        "random_state": 42,
        "n_jobs": -1
    }
    model = XGBRegressor(**params)
    scores = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=3, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    return -scores.mean()

xgb_study = optuna.create_study(direction="minimize", sampler=TPESampler(seed=42))
xgb_study.optimize(xgb_objective, n_trials=30, show_progress_bar=True)

xgb_model = XGBRegressor(**xgb_study.best_params, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
y_pred_train_xgb, y_pred_test_xgb, rmsle_xgb = evaluate_model(xgb_model, "XGBoost", X_train, y_train, X_test)

5.5 Create Submission¶

Creating submission file using the best performing model (based on training RMSLE).
